287. “On whom alone”: on the only male. For he had a sister Hippolyte, as Ibycus says (fr. 39 B. III 249).
288. “First loosed her girdle”: for women giving birth for the first time loosen their girdles and dedicate them to Artemis; hence also the sanctuary of Artemis the Girdle-loosener in Athens.

292. “Lamented”: mourned. Properly, “to lament” is used of a cow, and it is derived from “moving the tail” while lowing; and Apion, having found this etymology in Apollodorus (244 fr. 277 J.), that “bull” is derived from “stretching the tail,” transferred the discovery of the etymology.

299. “Though grieving, nevertheless”: that the conjunction “per” is often used instead of “ge” and “dē.” “Not even so, good though he is” (Iliad 1.131) thus: Aristarchus rendered it “being good indeed”; and “though he escaped sheer destruction” (Odyssey 17.47) “having escaped indeed.” Or the order is thus: though grieving in your heart over your fate, nevertheless endure to bear it.
